input.add_to_description: Day 11 ~3:40 PM: Brannoc is on the river road, first day of two; he camps near the Eel Fork milestone tonight.

entries.text:
Ansel presses the bread and the willow-bark into your hands, a twist of bitter bark that brews into a tea to cool a fever. You lay your palm on the green door and say the old blessing over it. He promises the book will keep a page for Reedholm.

On your question: Sedge is a good first name to ask for. He is the only one from Reedholm you know of, and he carried the sickness to the market, so he may be the best clue to how it started and who has it. But it's only one name. A village that has had no healer for half a year will have its own ideas about who is in charge, and you may find the headman or the ferry-boy first. Ask for Sedge, and listen to who answers.

The river road south is quiet. The valley widens and the hills flatten into pasture, then rough grass, then reed-beds with grey water standing between them. You walk steadily through the long afternoon. Herons lift off the shallows as you pass, and a wind from the south smells of mud and rot. Around mid-afternoon you reach a wooden milestone leaning in the verge, carved with an eel. This is the Eel Fork. A causeway of black timber and packed earth runs off east into the reeds, and the river road goes on south.

It's twenty to four on Day 11. You have four 1st-level and two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, two lanterns, rope, and thirty-seven flasks of oil. Reedholm is a day and a half down the causeway. The light is good for another two hours or more, then it will get cold and wet in the reeds.

What does Brannoc do?

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

input.add_to_description: Day 11: The Eel Fork milestone is carved on its back with seven mound-marks, each with a small lamp cut above it. Five lamps are scored through (Lamp, Long Cut, Drowned Stair, burial hill, Ford Chapel); two are not: a sixth in the row, and a seventh set apart under the east arrow toward Reedholm, the drowned barrow in the reeds. Old keepers lit lamps to hold the Chain shut.
Day 11 ~5 PM: A quarantine rope with red rags is strung across the causeway a quarter-mile east of the Eel Fork. A thin girl in a reed hat with a billhook keeps watch.

entries.text:
The Eel Fork is behind you, and Reedholm is two days away, not one. You've reached its quarantine rope on the first evening, but the causeway ahead is longer than the carters let on.

The girl in the reed hat is about fourteen, with a tight, tired face. She gets up as you near the rope and keeps the billhook low, not raised. She looks at your amulet and mace, and at the mud on your boots, and her voice cracks as she asks.

"Are you a healer? Say you're a healer."

input.add_to_description: Day 11 ~5 PM: Brannoc reaches the Eel Fork milestone and camps at a carters' lay-by, Reedholm another day ahead. Sedge is the first name to ask for (he is the reed-cutter's boy who carried the fever to market).

entries.text:
Ansel presses the willow-bark into your hand with the bread. It's a twist of dried strips, bitter to chew and good against a fever, and he tells you how to steep it. You bless the green door with a hand on the lintel. He says he'll keep a page open in the book for Reedholm, and that Edda's boy had better write.

The river road south is flat and wet, with reeds thickening on both sides as the hills fall away. You see herons and a heap of eel-pots at a landing, and few people. About five in the evening you reach the Eel Fork, a grey wooden milestone with a carved fish on its face. The east branch narrows into a raised causeway running out into reed-beds, which is the road to Reedholm. There's a carters' lay-by with a fire-ring and a lean-to, and you make camp there with your own fire and Hale's last apples. It's a long day's walk gone, and Reedholm is another day on.

Your question: yes, Sedge is the first name to ask for. He carried the fever to market and went home sick. If the sickness began with him, his household will tell you how it spread and who's worst off, and he is likely to be among the first who needs you. He is a reed-cutter's boy, so ask at the landing.

It's just after five on Day 11. You have all your slots, Channel Divinity, and 24 of 24 hit points. The light will hold for another hour. The causeway runs out ahead of you, the marsh is quiet, and the first pale mist is lifting off the water.

input.add_to_description: Day 11 ~4:40 PM: Brannoc passes the Eel Fork milestone and camps a mile up the east causeway; Reedholm lies a day further.

entries.text:
Ansel takes your hand at the green door, and you bless the lintel before you go. "The book will be open," he says. "Write, if you can. I like to know where my people are."

On Sedge: not necessarily first. He's a good name to ask for, since he's the boy who carried the fever to market, and his family will have seen it from the start. But a village with a marsh-fever has a worst-off house, and you can't know which it is until you look. Ask for Sedge, and ask who is sickest. Don't take only the first answer.

The road south is flat and wide, along the river, with willows and reed-beds crowding the bank. The air gets damper with every mile, and the light goes soft and pearly. You pass a cart or two, and a drover who nods at your amulet. Nobody speaks of Reedholm. By half past four you reach the Eel Fork, a grey wooden milestone leaning in the grass, with an eel carved crudely on the east face. The east branch is a raised causeway of packed earth and brushwood, running straight into the marsh. The reeds stand higher than your head on either side.

The light is going. You walk a mile up the causeway and find a dry knoll with a ring of old stones, where a fire has been lit before. The air smells of rot and water. A frog calls, and then a hundred. Your lantern makes a small yellow room in the dusk.

It's twenty to five on Day 11. Reedholm is a day's walk ahead, and tomorrow brings the Black Ford. You've four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and thirty-seven flasks. The moon is a thin sliver, and the night will be dark.

Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Prepare up to 6 spells from the whole cleric list after a long rest (domain spells are always prepared and don't count).
